data.text/markdown:
From a CSV File to a Dataframe

In this notebook you save the towns you read from the course API last week to a file, read them back, and answer one question about them three ways: with a loop, in polars and in SQL. Then you chart the answer.
✏️ Your turn. Add cells with the + button
🚀 This week's work
For a written answer, add a cell under the question, open the cell's ⋯ menu and choose Convert to Markdown. Every ✏️ is part of this week's work. The Going further at the end of an exercise is optional; try it once the rest is done.

Work with your agent the same way as in notebook 4. Try it yourself first, or write the steps in words. Then ask your agent, ask it to explain any line you could not have written, and ask which concepts its answer used. Exercise A is by hand.

1. Saving What You Fetched

The towns you read last week lived in memory, and they were gone when the notebook stopped. An API also changes. The shop takes new orders every day, and the tax figures change every year. Save a copy to a file, and the same analysis runs again on the same data, without a network, and anybody can open it in a spreadsheet. Mini Project 2 asks you to do the same. CSV is the plainest table a file can hold: one line per record, commas between the values, and a first line that names the columns. First, collect every town. /ma/counties lists the 14 counties.

get_towns is the function from notebook 4, section 2, with one change: per_page=100, because the largest county has 60 towns and the server sends 50 to a page unless you ask for more. Called once per county, it collects every town in the state.

Writing the file. Python's csv module writes and reads CSV files, so you never put the commas in yourself. csv.DictWriter takes a list of dictionaries, the shape you already have:
  • fieldnames names the columns to keep, in order. Each town has 14 fields, and extrasaction="ignore" leaves out the ones not named.
  • .writeheader() writes the first line, and .writerows() writes one line per town.
  • open(path, "w") opens the file for writing, and with closes it when the block ends. The empty newline setting is what the csv module asks for, so that lines end the same way on every computer.
A data file goes in the data folder, which sits in the root folder of your repository, one folder up from this notebook.

Open it. In VS Code's Explorer, the data folder now sits beside the notebooks folder, and ma-towns.csv is inside it. Click it: the table is plain text, one town per line. Reading it back. csv.DictReader reads one line at a time and turns each into a dictionary, with the header's names as keys. list(...) collects them all, and you are back to a list of records, the shape the API sent.

Every value the csv module reads is text. Look at the population: '49831', in quotes. A CSV file has no types, only characters, so the module gives you strings, and adding 1 to one raises a TypeError. int() turns it back into a number, or float() when it has a decimal point. The file does not record which columns were numbers, so you convert them yourself.

✏️ A · By Hand

No agent for this one, and no code completion either. When the editor suggests code in grey as you type, press Esc and keep typing your own. average_single_family_value_dollars is the state's figure for what a single-family home in the town is worth on average, as the town assesses it for tax. Call a town a million-dollar town when that figure is $1,000,000 or more. Across the state the middle town is near $586,000.
  1. How many million-dollar towns are there, and which county has the most of them? Use towns_from_file, a for loop, int(), and a dictionary that counts, as in notebook 3. Check yourself: 53 towns, and Middlesex has the most, with 14.
  2. Which town has the fewest people, and which has the most? Loop over towns_from_file and keep the smallest and the largest you have seen so far, the way find_largest did in notebook 4. Check yourself: Gosnold, with 62 people, and Boston, with 673,458.
Going further. Find the town with the most expensive average home in each county.

2. Describe What You Want

Your loops in A spelled out how: go through every town, convert, compare, add one or keep the smallest. That took a dozen lines, and a reader has to run them in their head to know what they answer. polars lets you describe what you want instead. pl.read_csv reads the same file into a DataFrame: a table with named columns. It is your list of records shown as a table, each row a record and each column a key, and polars has already turned the numbers into numbers.

data.text/markdown:
Here is A's first step in polars. Read it as a sentence:
  • .filter(...) keeps the million-dollar towns. It is the if in your loop, applied to every row at once, and pl.col(...) names the column it reads.
  • .group_by("county") makes one group per county, and .agg(pl.len()) counts the rows in each. It is your counting dictionary.
  • .sort(..., descending=True) puts the largest first.

data.text/markdown:
A count can mislead. Middlesex has the most million-dollar towns, and it also has 54 towns, more than any county but Worcester. The fairer question is what share of each county's towns are million-dollar towns.
  • pl.len() counts all the towns in each county.
  • A comparison such as pl.col(...) >= 1_000_000 is True or False for each town, and .sum() adds up the Trues, which counts them.
  • .with_columns() adds a column computed from the others, here one count divided by the other.

data.text/markdown: The share tells a different story from the count. Every town in Dukes County, which is Martha's Vineyard and the Elizabeth Islands, and in Nantucket is a million-dollar town, and nearly half of Barnstable's, which is Cape Cod. Middlesex comes sixth.

✏️ B · Check Against the Server

  1. Count every town per county with town_table, .group_by() and .agg(). The server counts them too, in ma_counties, and pl.DataFrame(ma_counties) turns that list of records into a table. Do the two agree? Check yourself: Worcester 60, Middlesex 54, Essex 34, and all 14 agree.
  2. Which five towns of more than 50,000 people have the highest average single-family bill? Use .filter(), .sort() and .head(). Check yourself: Brookline, Newton, Cambridge, Somerville, Quincy.
Going further. Ask the towns a question of your own that needs .filter(), .group_by() and .sort() together.

3. The Same Question in SQL

This is SQL, a second language, asking A's question once more. SQL is how databases are asked questions, and from next week the course builds and queries a database. For now, read it; you will write SQL in the database sessions. Behind a SQL cell is DuckDB, a database that runs inside the same Python as your notebook. The data stays in your DataFrames. When the cell runs, DuckDB looks up the name in the FROM line, here town_table, among the notebook's variables and reads that DataFrame as a table. Its answer comes back as a DataFrame too.

data.text/markdown: Read it top to bottom: SELECT names the columns of the answer, FROM the table, WHERE keeps some rows, GROUP BY makes one group per county, COUNT(*) counts each group, and ORDER BY ... DESC puts the largest first. Like the polars version, it describes what you want and leaves the how to the computer.

✏️ C · Raise the Bar

In the SQL cell, 1000000 is the bar a town's average home value has to reach. Before you change it to 2000000, predict in a markdown cell under this question: which counties' counts can go down, and can any go up? Then make the same change in the polars cell that counts million-dollar towns, and run both. Check yourself: both give Dukes, Middlesex and Norfolk 2 each and Nantucket 1, which is 7 towns. Going further. Write a SQL query of your own on town_table, and check its answer in polars.

4. The First Chart

Draw the share. .plot.bar() on a DataFrame draws one bar per row, with a library called altair. alt.X() and alt.Y() name each axis's column and give it a title a reader can understand, and .properties(title=...) states what the chart shows.
  • Putting the county on y lays the bars on their side, so every county's name reads across. sort="-x" puts the longest bar first.
  • axis=alt.Axis(format="%") writes a share of 0.25 as 25%.
Wrap it in mo.ui.altair_chart(), which is how marimo shows an altair chart of any size.
.plot.point() and .plot.line() work the same way. matplotlib is another charting library, and you will meet it in other people's code; Python §29 shows one chart in each.

✏️ D · A Chart of Your Own

Choose a question one chart can answer, from the data you saved for Mini Project 2 or from town_table. Draw it with titled axes, and a title that states what it shows. Check yourself: somebody who has not seen this notebook can say what each axis measures. Going further. Color the bars or dots by a column with color=, and explain what the colors add.
